Les personnes dévouées qui travaillent a: Dedicated people who work with and for their communities are a source of inspiration
J’estime que la joie autochtone se mêle: I believe Indigenous joy is intertwined with the laborious work of healing. I cherish every expression of it and consider it one of life’s highlights. My mother’s laughter is all the more striking for its contrast with the silence surrounding residential schools. Dedicated people who work with and for their communities are a source of inspiration. So I set out to listen to how they amplify, create and prioritize Indigenous joy.
Pour Kim Haxton, qui est Potéouatamis, l: For Kim Haxton, who is Potawatomi, Indigenous joy looks, sounds and smells like a connection to the land, or like smoke after singing around a fire. <l1>She works</l1> on developing land-based strategies for education, leadership and integration. Here is one of those sources of joy: “Ceremonies bring exuberance, children play, tough aunties laugh.”
La communauté est le fondement et la mot: Community is the foundation of, and the motivation behind, everything Cúagilákv <l1>Jess Housty</l1>, from the haíɫzaqv Nation, undertakes, whether it’s raising children, writing or community organizing. Their experience and their dual Heiltsuk and settler ancestry are constantly put to use in their work on food security, healing, land-based education and community-led social change.
« J’ai fait mes premières armes dans le: “I got my start in community work in a context of crisis, facing the extractive industry that threatened everything we held sacred. At the time, it was very easy to be carried along by anger, which was only a way of masking fear,” they explain. “But I always knew I wanted to dedicate my life to serving my people. I quickly understood that anger and fear wouldn’t let me pursue that goal over the long term,” Cúagilákv continues. “For about ten years now, every day, I get up and choose joy as my guide. It doesn’t erase the traumas of colonization or the difficult work I have to do, but it means I’m aiming for prosperity for future generations, which gives me a strong heart. By putting joy at the centre of my work, everything I do becomes a matter of healing, which feels fundamentally good and right.”
Teagan Pooyak, qui est Crie et Stoney, e: Teagan Pooyak, who is Cree and Stoney, embraces Indigenous joy.
Les enfants et les jeunes suscitent la j: Children and youth evoke joy eloquently. When Indigenous-led organizations prioritize it, that joy leads to healing. The underlying element inseparable from any progress is healing from the intergenerational trauma caused by residential schools. The <l1>Aboriginal Head Start Association of British Columbia</l1> (AHSABC) is a British Columbia organization whose provincial program allows preschool-aged children and their families living off reserve to experience, and receive the support of, a “village.” Director Joan Gignac explains that joy is the cornerstone of her work. “AHSABC programs bring children and Elders together to have fun, play, learn, share and grow. Knowing that Elders who went through residential schools didn’t have this experience as children, these activities are imbued with a sense of renewed joy,” she says.
Au <l1>Western Arctic Youth Collective</: At the <l1>Western Arctic Youth Collective</l1>, Indigenous joy is both a goal and a tool in every aspect of the collective’s work. Created by and for youth, WAYC offers participants in the Northwest Territories safe, inclusive spaces where they can express themselves, be themselves, learn, grow and make mistakes, which allows them to flourish. Coordinator Monica Loreen Dillon, who is Inuvialuk, explains it this way: “It creates a feeling of joy for those of us in the older generation too, by allowing our inner child to heal and by finding ourselves in these environments where we work with them.”
Enfin, <l1>IndigenEyez</l1> crée un espa: Finally, <l1>IndigenEyez</l1> creates a space for Indigenous people to come closer together, strengthen themselves and develop their leadership skills. Recognizing that reconciliation requires allies, Kelly Terbasket, of the Okanagan-Syilx Nation, created <l2>KinShift</l2>, where non-Indigenous people who want to tackle prejudice can gain the skills needed to build better relationships. For the founder, the term “Indigenous” refers to thousands of years of connection to the land, which confers the wisdom to be a relative of the land, a strand in the web, rather than placing human beings first or exercising domination. “This relationship is founded on respect, compassion, care and reverence. Joy is one of the things that flow from being so intimately connected to all our relations,” says the program director. In her view, Indigenous joy is the opposite of restriction and reflects limitless potential.
Chehala Leonard, cinéaste aseniwuche win: Chehala Leonard, an Aseniwuche Winewak filmmaker and producer at the National Film Board of Canada (NFB), believes joy comes from askîy (the land). “Being out on the land with filmmakers brings me the greatest joy. In a word, it grounds me, reminds me where I come from and gives me the chance to honour the work we do together,” she says.
L’écrivain anichinabé Waubgeshig Rice ab: Anishinaabe writer Waubgeshig Rice echoes this. “Indigenous joy is a key element of my work, whether it’s seeking it out, highlighting it or generating it. So many generations were deprived of joy, and now that we’re able to promote it and revel in it, I want to do my best to share it,” he says.
Le travail de la photographe blackfoot e: The work of Blackfoot and Cree photographer <l1>Mary Big Bull</l1> celebrates Indigeneity: “It’s about reclaiming what was stolen from the generations before us. It’s embracing Indigenous identity as a whole and being proud of that part of ourselves, celebrating Indigenous culture in ways we couldn’t before,” the photographer says. In this way, she shows the beauty of the skin, hair and eye colour of the dancers and of the regalia, all elements that have too long been perceived negatively.
Lily Big Bull Holloway, à la fois Siksi: Lily Big Bull Holloway, both Siksika and Blackfoot, represents a new generation of Indigenous joy. Photo by Mary Big Bull
L’<l1>artiste</l1> Jada-Gabrielle Pape,: <l1>Artist</l1> Jada-Gabrielle Pape, who is Saanich and Snuneymuxw, is also a certified <l2>counsellor</l2> and coach. Her most intimate work is as a counsellor and coach, while her strategic and systemic work is as a facilitator and consultant in decolonization and anti-racism, which she does with organizations. Before speaking about joy, she refers to her roots. “My life’s work is shaped by the family, community, Elders and knowledge keepers I come from and belong to,” she says.
« Beaucoup d’entre eux sont décédés avan: “Many of them died before having the chance to live all the things they taught us and fought for. So I see it as both my privilege and my responsibility to live their legacy. My daily intention is not only to fight for justice, but to embody it, not just to talk about love and justice,” the artist continues, before leaving us with these words: “I know, deep down, that this heals my ancestors and carries on their wishes for the world they wanted for all of us,” she concludes.
